requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) configured to provide NAT/masquerade egress for the 10.50.50.0/24 private subnet, implemented via an Ansible playbook
requirements.summary: An Ansible playbook (site.yml, run from control node node4) templates a VyOS configuration script and applies it via ansible.builtin.command with become, setting eth1=10.50.50.254/24 and a source-NAT masquerade rule for 10.50.50.0/24 out eth0, then commits/saves. A later idempotent re-run of the same playbook (cmd-6e59e59fff8545e5) confirms the config is fully described and reproducible by Ansible ('already exists' for the address/NAT lines). The nft ruleset on node1 (cmd-e253f5e052524a6d) shows the live masquerade rule with nonzero packet/byte counters, and ip_forward=1 is enabled. Note: the exact CLI syntax was first discovered via manual SSH/bash troubleshooting after the vyos.vyos.vyos_config module failed against this VyOS build's interactive CLI; that discovered script was then folded into the final Ansible playbook that manages it idempotently going forward.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 configured (via Ansible) with a route to the internet through node1's private-network address
requirements.summary: The same Ansible playbook uses community.general.nmcli to give node2/node3 static IPs (10.50.50.11/.12) on enp8s0 with node1 (10.50.50.254) as a lower-priority default gateway (metric 200), plus ansible.posix.sysctl to disable rp_filter on that NIC (persisted to /etc/sysctl.d, confirmed by cmd-7548e8a43e414d6e / cmd-e376b8d4a3b34f60). Playbook run cmd-c069a129d7d14bd8/cmd-6e59e59fff8545e5 show changed=true for these tasks with no failures.

requirements.requirement: End-to-end internet egress from node2 and node3 through node1's NAT is functionally demonstrated
requirements.summary: After the rp_filter root cause was diagnosed and fixed via the Ansible sysctl task, ping (0% loss) and HTTPS curl (HTTP 301) from both node2 and node3 succeeded via enp8s0/private gateway; tcpdump on node1 eth0 and eth1 plus conntrack show the outbound packets translated and matched via the masquerade rule, corroborating the client-observed success rather than relying on the client claim alone.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart boot identity/health, restart, changed post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state for all managed nodes
requirements.summary: For all four nodes, boot_id was captured before restart, a reboot was triggered, connectivity loss/timeout was observed during the transition, and a differing boot_id was captured after recovery. Post-restart, node1's NAT rule/eth1 address/ip_forward were re-verified, node2/node3's static IP, rp_filter=0 persistence, and live ping/HTTPS through NAT were re-verified (confirming persisted sysctl config survived reboot), and node4 (control node) had ansible-core intact with successful ansible ping to all three other nodes. The fixed after-executor lifecycle boot-identity snapshots for all four nodes match the command-level boot_id values, cross-confirming the transition.

overall_summary: The executor implemented NAT egress for node2/node3 through node1 as an Ansible playbook (site.yml on the control node4), with the VyOS interface address and source-NAT masquerade rule, and RHEL client static IPs plus rp_filter fixes, all managed as idempotent Ansible tasks confirmed by a clean final playbook run. End-to-end egress (ping 0% loss, HTTPS 301) was directly verified from both node2 and node3, corroborated by nft counters, tcpdump, and conntrack on node1, with the rp_filter root cause correctly diagnosed and fixed. The mandatory node-restart protocol was completed for all four nodes with boot_id before/after evidence and full functional recovery, including persistence of the NAT and sysctl configuration across node1's reboot. Minor, bounded VyOS CLI troubleshooting mutations occurred during diagnosis of a broken Ansible module path; one was fully reverted and one was a no-op, and temporary artifacts were cleaned up.
limitations: The eth1 address and NAT masquerade rule were first applied to node1 via manual SSH/bash script execution while diagnosing a vyos.vyos.vyos_config module incompatibility with this VyOS build's CLI, before being encoded into the final Ansible playbook; the playbook's idempotent 'already exists' confirmation demonstrates it now fully describes and can reproduce this state, but the very first application was not itself performed by Ansible.
Command outputs are bounded/truncated in places (e.g., long nmcli attribute dumps), so some deep configuration detail beyond what's quoted could not be independently reviewed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were clearly tied to the goal: SSH key provisioning for Ansible connectivity, collection installs, the final idempotent Ansible playbook runs, and diagnostic rp_filter toggles that were folded into a persistent Ansible task. Two bounded troubleshooting mutations on node1's VyOS config were not directly load-bearing for the final solution: (1) cmd-8172f6d20cf949b1 set 'system host-name node1' via an ad-hoc vyos_config test to probe module behavior — value was unchanged from the existing hostname so it left no meaningful residue; (2) cmd-0f0d79e820e54299 set an eth1 'description sudo-test-ok' via a manual sudo script to diagnose why config sessions failed over plain SSH — this was fully reverted by cmd-f015d88aae44430c (delete description, commit, save), confirmed removed by a subsequent showCfg. Several other VyOS CLI experiments (description 'testme', address 10.50.50.1/24, interactive configure attempts) failed outright ('Set failed'/'Invalid command') and made no state change. Temporary debug/apply scripts on node1 (/tmp/vyos_test.sh, vyos_debug.sh, vyos_debug2.sh, vyos_apply.sh, vyos_cleanup.sh) and tcpdump/conntrack log files were explicitly removed at the end (cmd-f015d88aae44430c, cmd-a0ff618f0e134453). The after-executor lifecycle snapshot shows no abandoned files, failed services, or package-health issues beyond expected session-scoped systemd-private directories tied to the new boot IDs.
